claims.claim: Nutritional needs shift across life stages, so eating well means matching food choices to the stage of life (the working definition of lifespan nutrition).

MyPlate, the USDA's food guidance program, organizes healthy eating by life stage, with pages for pregnancy and breastfeeding, infants, toddlers, kids, teens, adults, and older adults, and states that at every stage of life it is never too early or too late to eat healthy.

The six life stages taught in this lesson each carry different nutritional needs: infancy's rapid growth, childhood's steady growth and habit-building, adolescence's growth spurt, adulthood's maintenance tied to activity, pregnancy's support of fetal development, and older age's lower calorie needs with continued nutrient needs.
Nutritional needs change because of four forces: growth, development, activity, and aging, each of which shifts demands across life stages.
The general pattern: needs are high relative to body size while bodies are growing, and in older age calorie needs often decline while the need for nutrient-dense foods stays important.
The honest note: the exact make-up of a healthy diet varies with individual characteristics such as age, gender, lifestyle, and degree of physical activity, so no single eating plan fits everyone.
Eating well at every stage means choosing nutrient-dense foods across and within the food groups, with amounts adjusted to the stage and to calorie needs.

Infants need food for energy and nutrients; breast milk is best for the first months and provides the necessary vitamins and minerals, infant formulas are available, and solid foods usually begin around six months of age.
The honest framing: consuming a healthy diet throughout the life course supports health at every stage, making nutrition a lifelong, adjustable conversation with the body rather than a one-time fix.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The subject source-map described OpenStax Nutrition ch. 14 as the lifespan chapter; the current edition (Jan 2026 update) is organized by body system, with 'across the lifespan' sections inside system chapters, so no single lifespan chapter exists to cite.
positions: Current OpenStax Nutrition for Nurses 2e: system-organized
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Cited OpenStax Section 1.1's verified definition ('nutrition is the intake of food to meet the needs of the body') and anchored the lifespan framing on MyPlate life stages, WHO life-course framing, NIA older-adult guidance, and MedlinePlus infant facts instead.

conflictingEvidence.issue: 'Higher needs per pound while growing' is a general physiological pattern; none of the verified sources states it verbatim with numbers.
positions: Pattern stated generally in the lesson as part of its core
Sources verify the components: infants need energy and nutrients for growth (MedlinePlus), needs vary with age and physical activity (WHO), calorie needs change with age and activity (NIA)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Stated as a simple general pattern without quantitative per-pound figures, supported by the verified component claims.

sourceRecords.title: Healthy Diet (fact sheet)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22 (fact sheet dated 26 January 2026). Supports: consuming a healthy diet throughout the life course helps prevent malnutrition in all its forms and noncommunicable diseases; the exact make-up of a healthy diet varies with individual characteristics (e.g. age, gender, lifestyle and degree of physical activity), cultural context, local foods, and dietary customs.

sourceRecords.title: Healthy Eating (NIA health topic)
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute on Aging (NIA), National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Tier A. 'Healthy eating is a cornerstone of healthy aging'; guidance to choose a variety of nutrient-dense foods across and within all the food groups (vegetables, fruits, grains, protein foods, dairy products, and oils).

sourceRecords.title: How Much Should I Eat? Quantity and Quality
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute on Aging (NIA), National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Tier A. Calorie needs vary with age, sex, and physical activity; DGA-based daily calorie suggestions for people over 60 (women about 1,600-2,200, men about 2,000-2,600 depending on activity); 'getting the proper nutrients and eating the right amount for your weight and activity level can contribute to healthy aging.'

sourceRecords.title: Healthy Eating As You Age: Know Your Food Groups
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute on Aging (NIA), National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Tier A. The amount you should eat to maintain your weight depends on your age, sex, and level of physical activity; food groups described per the Dietary Guidelines for Americans; importance of getting the recommended amount of each food group without going over daily recommended calories.

sourceRecords.title: Infant and Newborn Nutrition
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Tier A. Food provides the energy and nutrients babies need; breast milk is best and has all the necessary vitamins and minerals; infant formulas are available; infants are usually ready to eat solid foods at about 6 months of age.

sourceRecords.title: Nutrition for Nurses, Section 1.1: What Is Nutrition?
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture (2025) of the canonical OpenStax URL. Provides the working definition 'Nutrition is the intake of food to meet the needs of the body' and the macronutrient/micronutrient framing.
